analysis.one_liner: Shields businesses from federal lawsuits over customers' or workers' COVID-19 deaths and disabilities.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced May 1, 2020 and referred to three House committees, it received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal commission to issue voluntary COVID-19 safety guidance for businesses, then used that guidance as a legal shield: a worker, customer, or family member could not sue a business in federal court over a COVID-19 death or disability if the business followed the guidance, unless they first sent written notice and gave the business time to fix the problem. It also would have pushed COVID-19 claims toward mediation instead of court, and given states that passed similar lawsuit limits priority in certain Small Business Administration loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Business owners and operators, especially small businesses, who would gain protection from federal lawsuits claiming a COVID-19 death or disability was caused by unsafe practices at the business. State governments adopting similar lawsuit limits would get priority treatment for certain SBA general business loans. Mediation and arbitration providers would gain a new stream of referred claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Business owners facing COVID-19 liability suits

how_it_helps.text: A person could not sue a business under federal law for a COVID-19 death or disability if the business followed national or state guidance aligned with the bill's commission recommendations, unless they first gave written notice of the unsafe practice and the business failed to respond or fix it within a deadline set by the commission.

The Judicial Conference would develop a mediation and alternative dispute resolution program for federal COVID-19 liability claims, including a stay of discovery during mediation, aimed at resolving claims without costly litigation.

The Small Business Administration would give priority, in certain 7(a) general business loans, to borrowers in states that enact laws substantially similar to the bill's liability limits and mediation program.

The CDC, working with a new COVID-19 Response Commission, would educate state and local governments and business owners on strategies to minimize COVID-19 exposure for employees, customers, and vulnerable populations.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, customers, and the families of people who died or became disabled from COVID-19 at a business, who would face a notice-and-cure requirement and a compliance shield before they could reach federal court. Trial lawyers and plaintiffs in these cases would lose the most direct route to recovery. The public also bears the risk that a business technically following voluntary guidance escapes accountability even when someone dies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick or bereaved workers and customers

drawbacks.text: The bill bars federal suits whenever a business adheres to the guidance, so a business could follow the letter of voluntary standards and avoid liability even if a worker or customer dies of COVID-19 on its premises.

The lawsuit bar applies only after a notice-and-cure process with deadlines set by the commission, meaning sick or bereaved people would have to document and formally notify a business and wait out a cure period before filing, delaying or deterring claims.

The definition of 'national guidance' is frozen at the date a state begins reopening small businesses closed by executive order, so the legal shield could rest on outdated standards rather than the CDC's best current advice, and the commission that sets the standards includes business owners and a White House economic task force alongside health officials.
Mediation with a stay of discovery would let a business postpone the document demands that usually reveal what safety steps it actually took, weakening plaintiffs' ability to prove their case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Businesses facing a novel pandemic-era lawsuit risk had a real concern, and the education program is uncontroversial. But the core trade is one-sided: it trades away the legal recourse of people who died or were disabled from COVID-19 at a business in exchange for protection framed around guidance compliance, with the shield potentially keyed to reopening-day standards rather than current science. The bill died without a vote, so none of these effects took place.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Burchett introduced the Coronavirus Public Safety and Economic Recovery Act on May 1, 2020, during the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and additionally to the Judiciary and Small Business Committees; that referral was the last action the bill ever received.
Six House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 with the bill still pending in committee, so the liability shield, mediation program, and SBA loan priority never took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, workers, customers, and surviving families kept their existing ability to bring federal suits over COVID-19 deaths and disabilities, and business owners gained no new shield. The bill's small group of supporters got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers and families kept their right to sue

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral on May 1, 2020 — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; its jurisdiction covered the lawsuit-limiting provisions.

against.name: House Small Business Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; its jurisdiction covered the SBA loan priority provision.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all six cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so the parties never took a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Retail, hospitality, and other customer-facing businesses
industries.note: The bill would give these employers a shield against federal lawsuits over COVID-19 deaths and disabilities whenever they follow government-issued safety guidance, with a notice-and-cure hurdle before any suit. That protection comes directly out of the legal recourse of sick workers, customers, and bereaved families.

A broad category of COVID-19 liability claims would become much harder to bring, and those that survive would be steered into mediation. Their loss is the business community's gain, with ordinary people's recovery claims in between.

industries.industry: Mediation and alternative dispute resolution providers
industries.note: A Judicial Conference model program would route federal COVID-19 claims toward mediation, creating work for neutrals and ADR providers. Whether this serves claimants depends on the program's design.
Owners in states that copied the bill's liability limits would get priority for certain SBA 7(a) general business loans, using federal credit access as an incentive for states to limit lawsuits.
